group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: sorted array: find a pair or triple with a given sum
because: Sortedness is the enabling property: moving left can only raise the sum, moving right can only lower it, so each step eliminates a whole row of the search space. Unsorted, this is a hashmap problem instead.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: subarray or substring of a size that is given to you
because: The size is not being searched for, so there is no shrink condition: add the entering element, remove the leaving element, and slide.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: longest or shortest subarray such that…, all values non-negative
because: Non-negativity is what makes shrinking sound: extending can only push the sum up, shrinking can only pull it down, so the window has a monotone relationship with the constraint. Negatives destroy this and force a prefix-sum approach.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: count subarrays summing to exactly k, and negatives are possible
reach_for: Prefix sum + hashmap: a window cannot work
because: Negatives destroy the monotonicity a window needs; extending can lower the sum and shrinking can raise it, so no two-pointer invariant holds. A prefix-sum lets you ask ‘how many earlier prefix sums equal current − k?’ in O(1) per step.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: exactly K distinct / exactly K odd numbers
because: ‘Exactly’ is not directly windowable, but ‘at most’ is monotone in window length: adding elements never decreases the distinct count, so a valid shrink condition exists. Subtract atMost(K−1) from atMost(K) to isolate the exact count.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: max or min over every window of a fixed size k
because: A heap gives you the max but cannot evict the element that just left the window; a heap update would be O(n) per step. The deque maintains a decreasing sequence of indices so the front is always the window’s maximum and eviction is O(1).

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: in-place removal, partition, or reversal over one array
reach_for: Two pointers in the same direction: a slow write index behind a fast read index
because: There is no interval invariant here, so it is not a window at all; nothing is being summed or counted across a range. The slow pointer marks where the next valid element should land; the fast pointer scans ahead to find it.

says: return the best value, and you can say why a local choice is safe
because: The test is the exchange argument: can any optimal solution be transformed to agree with the greedy choice without getting worse? If yes, greedy is correct. If you cannot construct that argument, reach for DP instead.

says: a locally worse choice can pay off later
reach_for: DP: and the state must carry whatever the choice affects
because: Greedy fails exactly when choices interact across steps. That interaction is the state: whatever a future step needs to know about what you did, encode it explicitly in the DP dimension.

says: how many ways / count the arrangements
because: Greedy returns one solution. Counting needs every branch aggregated, which is what the DP recurrence does: the count at state s is the sum of the counts at every state that transitions to s.

says: fewest coins or steps to reach a target, denominations arbitrary
because: Largest-first is only safe for canonical coin systems. With arbitrary denominations a greedy pick can block a shorter path; the DP over every target amount 0…T finds the true minimum by checking every denomination at each step.

says: intervals: keep the most non-overlapping ones
because: Earliest finishing time leaves the most room for everything after it, and that exchange argument is exact: any optimal solution that does not pick the earliest-ending interval can be modified to do so without losing a slot.

says: “with a cooldown”, “at most k transactions”
because: The constraint is a mode you are in rather than a quantity you accumulate, so the recurrence branches on which state you are transitioning from. Cooldown adds a ‘resting’ state; transaction limits add a count dimension.

says: return ALL subsets / permutations / valid paths
because: You need the objects themselves, so the output is exponential and no table can compress it. Backtracking generates each object once, pruning branches that cannot lead to valid completions.

says: return the COUNT, or the BEST, of those same objects
because: You need only an aggregate, so overlapping subproblems can be collapsed rather than re-expanded. The exponential search space becomes polynomial because each subproblem is solved once and its answer reused.

says: shortest path, every edge costs 1
reach_for: BFS: multi-source if there are several origins
because: Uniform cost makes layer order the same as distance order, so first arrival is optimal and no relaxation is needed. Multi-source BFS initialises the queue with all sources simultaneously, giving the distance to the nearest source in one pass.

says: shortest path with weights, but at most k hops
reach_for: Bellman–Ford / DP over hop count: NOT Dijkstra
because: Dijkstra finalises a node the first time it is popped, which is wrong once a longer path with fewer hops is preferable. The hop limit is a second dimension: dp[k][v] = cheapest cost to reach v in exactly k steps.

says: “minimise the maximum”, “maximise the minimum”, “largest k that still works”
reach_for: Binary search on the answer + a feasibility check
because: The answer is monotone (if k is feasible then everything easier is too), so you can binary-search the value space and reduce the problem to a yes/no feasibility check at each midpoint. The check is usually a greedy or a linear scan.

says: top k from a stream, or n is huge and k is small
because: Sorting is n log n and needs all the data at once; a k-heap is n log k and works online. For top-k largest, keep a min-heap of size k: if the new element beats the heap’s minimum, evict and insert.

says: prefix matching across many words
because: A hashset answers exact membership only. Prefixes need the shared structure a trie provides: all words with the same prefix share the same root-to-node path, so a prefix query is a single traversal rather than scanning every word.

says: “are these connected”, “merge these groups”, and no path is asked for
because: It answers connectivity without producing a path, which is why it beats BFS/DFS when you only need the yes/no and need to handle many merge operations cheaply. Path compression and union by rank make both operations nearly O(1) amortised.

says: array of n values that all lie in the range [1,n]: find what is missing or duplicated, in O(1) extra space
reach_for: Use the index as the hash: put each value at position value−1, or negate the slot it points to
because: The constraint that values fit the index range is the whole hint: the array can act as its own presence table. Negating a slot marks a value as seen without a separate array; a missing positive after the pass is the answer.

says: compute aⁿ, or divide/multiply without using the operator, with n as large as 1e9
reach_for: Halve the exponent: square and recurse, handling the odd step
because: Linear repetition is 1e9 operations; halving is 30. Distinct from binary search on the answer: here you are computing a value, not searching for one. The odd-step handler (multiply by base once) is the only branch.

says: process a number or expression by its structure: digits group in chunks, operators have precedence, brackets nest
reach_for: Recursion with a base case per unit: solve the smallest chunk directly, combine upward
because: The problem has natural size boundaries that define the recursion. A number splits into groups of three digits with scale words (thousands, millions); an expression splits at operators by precedence; brackets define nesting depth. Identify the smallest unit that resolves directly, write one level of the recursion, and trust the call stack for the rest. A stack can simulate this when the recursion is too deep or when an iterative pass is clearer.
